steps.title: Order matters or not?
steps.content: A permutation counts arrangements where order matters. A combination counts selections where order does not matter. First ask: would swapping two selected items create a different outcome?
steps.example: Choosing captain and vice-captain from 5 people is a permutation. Choosing any 2 team members is a combination.

steps.title: Choose the right operation
steps.prompt: A team of 3 students is selected from 8. Which method should be used?
steps.explanation: The team is the same regardless of the order in which the 3 students are chosen, so use combinations.

steps.title: Use the formulas
steps.content: nPr = n!/(n−r)! counts ordered arrangements. nCr = n!/[r!(n−r)!] counts unordered selections.

steps.title: Calculate a combination
steps.prompt: How many ways can 2 people be selected from 6 people?

steps.title: Watch for repeated positions
steps.content: If all n distinct items are arranged, the number of arrangements is n!. If some positions have restrictions, count the allowed choices stage by stage.
steps.example: Four different books on a shelf can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways.

questions.prompt: How many ways can 4 distinct books be arranged?
For a combination, does the order of selected items matter?
questions.explanation: A combination treats a selection as the same regardless of order.
